Memory summary

This unit established the task contract and prepared a working development environment. The agent inspected the reference, baseline, checker, benchmark, and problem prompt; discovered that the default Python and available virtual environments lacked Torch; then installed Torch 2.11.0+cu128 and Triton 3.6.0 in a problem-local venv. A basic CUDA operation succeeded on an H100 PCIe with capability 9.0 and 114 SMs. No solution kernel, correctness check, or benchmark score was produced in this unit.

Relevant prior context

The pre-unit skim of lines 1–3 returned no events. Line 4 begins with a session-start record in the 02_kimi_linear_decode problem directory. The agent was using deepseek/deepseek-v4-flash-0731; the task requested an implementation in solution.py.

Important non-obvious context
  • The requested target in the problem prompt is an RTX PRO 6000 (SM120 Blackwell, 1.8 TB/s GDDR7), but the available device was an H100 PCIe. Hardware-specific performance conclusions would therefore need qualification.
  • The system Python was 3.12.3 and could not import Torch or Triton. /opt/python-venv and the user venv also lacked Torch. A cached Torch directory was for CPython 3.11, so it was not directly usable by the system Python.

  • The benchmark score is baseline latency divided by solution latency, geometrically averaged over contexts 2048, 8192, and 16384. Despite the field name peak_fraction, it is a speedup multiple.

Recording summary

The agent began by listing the problem directory and reading the supplied files. The reference specifies a batch-1 repeating motif of three KDA blocks followed by one MLA block, each with a 64-expert MoE. Hidden size is 2304; KDA uses 32 heads of dimension 128 and a convolution window of four; MLA uses a 512-wide latent cache, 128 non-RoPE key dimensions, 64 RoPE dimensions, and 128 value dimensions. Projection weights use asymmetric group-128 int4 quantization, packed two values per uint8 along the input dimension. The reference materializes dequantized weights; the intended optimization is to fuse unpacking, dequantization, and GEMV.

The agent then read the baseline and harness files. The baseline also materializes dequantized bf16 weights, while the checker enforces strict state-dict compatibility and checks updated state as well as hidden output. The benchmark runs 32 decode steps at context 2048 and 16 steps at 8192 and 16384, with three performance trials. The prompt and problem.yaml make the single-kernel constraint and import restrictions explicit.

Initial environment probes failed because default Python lacked Torch and Triton. The agent searched common virtual environments and the UV cache, checked the Python version and network access, inspected the harness wrappers, and created a Python 3.12 venv. The install completed with:

Measuring CUDA cooperative grid synchronization for the fused decode kernel

Measuring CUDA cooperative grid synchronization for the fused decode kernel
Memory summary

After confirming that an inline CUDA extension worked, the agent tested whether CUDA cooperative groups could provide the global stage barrier needed by the planned fused decode kernel. A proper cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel test ran repeated grid.sync() calls and measured 1.582 μs per synchronization at G=456 and 1.140 μs at G=912. This was faster than the earlier Triton sense-reversing barrier prototype’s roughly 2.1–2.7 μs, but still a meaningful cost if the fused forward pass required many barriers.

Relevant prior context

The run had moved from Triton barrier experiments to a CUDA extension because the intended design was a staged cooperative kernel: blocks would process parts of each stage, with grid.sync() between stages. The inline extension compiled and returned OK True. Immediately before this unit, the agent decided to verify cooperative launch support and barrier cost on the actual GPU.

Important non-obvious context

The task specified an RTX PRO 6000, but the available device was an H100 PCIe. The trace detected Triton 3.6.0, CUDA 12.8, compute capability 9.0, and 114 SMs. Correctness was still PASS at this point; no official benchmark score had been recorded. The benchmark’s official target requires one custom GPU kernel launch for the full decode step, while the requested performance score is a speedup multiple over baseline.

Recording summary

The first test script was explicitly abandoned: it created an argument array incorrectly and did not actually issue a valid cooperative launch. The agent then wrote a corrected test using cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel, passing pointers to the output pointer and iteration count:

void* args[] = {&optr, &iters};
int threads = 256;
int blocks = G / threads;
cudaLaunchCooperativeKernel((void*)coop_kernel, dim3(blocks), dim3(threads), args, 0, 0);

The kernel obtained a cooperative grid group with cg::this_grid() and called grid.sync() in a loop. The Python harness warmed up the launch, synchronized the device, timed another 100 barrier iterations, and reported microseconds per synchronization:

G=456: 1.582 us per grid.sync
G=912: 1.140 us per grid.sync

These measurements established that cooperative grid synchronization worked in the extension on this H100. Its measured cost was lower than the preceding Triton barrier measurements, supporting continued investigation of the cooperative staged-kernel approach, while making the number of required global barriers an important performance consideration.

  • Contribution: Measured CUDA grid synchronization at roughly 1.14–1.58 μs per barrier on the H100; no official score was produced.
  • Takeaway: The measurement justified considering cooperative groups, but the final grid synchronization did not protect all within-stage shared global updates.

Important non-obvious context

The task specifies an RTX PRO 6000, but this trace’s environment was an H100 PCIe (compute capability 9.0, 114 SMs). The prototype lived in /tmp/dev/gemv_proto.py; it was a standalone GEMV experiment, not the fused solution.py step kernel. Its Python timing loop used perf_counter, called a wrapper that allocates an output tensor each time, warmed up five calls, and timed 100 calls before synchronizing. Thus the reported bandwidth is the script’s effective estimate, not a clean measurement of device-only memory throughput.

The packed weights were stored as [in/2, out] bytes, with each byte holding two int4 values along the input dimension. The prototype assigned threads to output columns, so adjacent lanes read contiguous weight columns for each packed input row.

Recording summary

At line 160, the agent worked through the fused-kernel dependency graph. It counted five synchronization boundaries for each KDA layer and nine for MLA plus its MoE, totaling 24. It considered reducing barriers with finer-grained readiness flags or redundant computation, but judged both approaches less attractive than global grid synchronization. The agent chose CUDA over Triton for control of the cooperative launch and memory access patterns, then planned a column-parallel GEMV prototype.

At lines 161–162, the agent created /tmp/dev/gemv_proto.py. The CUDA kernel assigned one thread to each output column, iterated over groups of 128 inputs, unpacked each byte into low and high nibbles, dequantized with per-group bf16 scales and zeros, and accumulated the dot product. The first test script failed while constructing quantized weights: its zeros expression mixed a [18,1,4096] minimum tensor with a [18,4096] scale tensor, causing an unintended extra dimension.

The agent checked the shapes with a smaller script. The diagnostic showed:

w torch.Size([2304, 4096]) wg torch.Size([18, 128, 4096]) wmin torch.Size([18, 1, 4096]) scales torch.Size([18, 4096]) zeros torch.Size([18, 18, 4096])

The fix was to keep scale and zero tensors in [groups,1,out] form during quantization, then squeeze the group-internal dimension for the kernel inputs. The revised script used:

scales3 = (wmax - wmin).clamp_min(1e-8) / 15.0
zeros3 = (-wmin / scales3).round().clamp(0, 15)
scales = scales3.squeeze(1).to(T.bfloat16)
zeros = zeros3.squeeze(1).to(T.bfloat16)
wq_f = ((wg / scales3) + zeros3).round().clamp(0,15)

At lines 172–175, the revised prototype ran across several block and thread configurations. All eight reported nearly identical latency and bandwidth, with small relative error:

blocks=32 threads=256: 132.69 us, BW=38 GB/s, relerr=8.48e-07
blocks=64 threads=256: 132.08 us, BW=38 GB/s, relerr=8.48e-07
blocks=128 threads=256: 132.34 us, BW=38 GB/s, relerr=8.48e-07
blocks=256 threads=256: 132.26 us, BW=38 GB/s, relerr=8.48e-07
blocks=64 threads=128: 132.79 us, BW=38 GB/s, relerr=8.48e-07
blocks=128 threads=128: 132.79 us, BW=38 GB/s, relerr=8.48e-07
blocks=256 threads=128: 132.87 us, BW=38 GB/s, relerr=8.48e-07
blocks=512 threads=128: 132.80 us, BW=38 GB/s, relerr=8.48e-07

The unit ended with a numerically accurate but slow standalone GEMV. The measurements did not yet explain why block count and thread count had almost no effect; the next unit tested alternative grouping and loading strategies.

Fixing MoE pointer ordering after gate/up stage crashes
Memory summary

Repeated staged launches completed through stage 4, then failed at stage 5. The investigation found that Python packed MoE pointers per layer, while the CUDA parameter setup expected them grouped by projection type across all four layers. Reordering the host pointers fixed the mismatch: the subsequent stage sweep completed stages 1 through 6. No benchmark score was recorded in this unit.

Relevant prior context

The run was building a single cooperative CUDA kernel for the four-block decode step. Previous attempts had repeatedly encountered illegal accesses in later stages. Immediately before this unit, a stage sweep still failed at stage 5. The agent had also been changing gate/up weighting and testing launch bounds, so it considered both kernel scheduling and memory indexing as possible causes.

Important non-obvious context

The trace ran on an H100, with Triton 3.6.0, CUDA 12.8, capability 9.0, and 114 SMs. Although the task specified an RTX PRO 6000, this run used the available H100.

The official score was still None before and after this unit. The recorded correctness status remained PASS; the staged launches below were debugging checks, not a new benchmark result. The unit changed solution.py by +9/−6 lines.

The host and device pointer layouts differed:

  • Python had appended each layer’s gate, up, down, and shared-expert pointers with each projection’s weight, scale, and zero pointers interleaved.
  • The CUDA setup expected pointer groups by projection key: for each key, all four layers’ weight pointers, then all scales, then all zeros.

This mismatch could make the gate/up stage read invalid pointers. The fix explicitly matched the CUDA layout:

# NOTE: append order must match _ORDER in kernels/build.py:
# per key (g,u,d,sg,su,sd): all wq (4 layers), then all s, then all z.
for key in ("gate", "up", "down", "s_gate", "s_up", "s_down"):
    for l in range(4):
        P.append(getattr(moe[l], key).w_q.data_ptr())
    for l in range(4):
        P.append(getattr(moe[l], key).scales.data_ptr())
    for l in range(4):
        P.append(getattr(moe[l], key).zeros.data_ptr())

The final submission implemented the full batch-1 decode step as a handwritten CUDA cooperative megakernel, launched once from Model.step. Relevant prior context

The task required one custom GPU launch for the entire forward step, with packed int4 weights, bf16 group scales and zeros, recurrent KDA state, and an expanding MLA cache. The run developed an inline CUDA extension and used cooperative grid.sync() barriers between 28 stages. The Python Model.step prepared a live pointer table and scratch buffers, then called ext.run_step once.

Several implementation details were corrected during development: router weights were transposed and retained; the pointer table was reordered to match the CUDA kernel’s expected per-key layout (all weights, then scales, then zeros); and the MLA Z scratch buffer was expanded to 32 elements. A faulty routed gate/up GEMV was replaced with gemv_atomic<4>, after which the isolated MoE output matched the reference closely. These local fixes did not resolve the full-step failure.

The available GPU was an H100, not the specified RTX PRO 6000. The baseline measured 11.282, 11.565, and 12.406 ms/token at contexts 2048, 8192, and 16384 on the H100 PCIe. These are baseline measurements only; the official solution benchmark did not run after correctness failed.

Recording summary

The final Python solution defines the model’s quantized projections, KDA and MLA blocks, MoE layers, state preparation, and pointer table. step(hidden, state) prepares or refreshes pointers, invokes ext.run_step once, then publishes the appended MLA cache views. The CUDA extension performs handwritten int4 unpacking and asymmetric dequantization and executes all stages behind cooperative grid barriers.

The audit traced the failed output to two scratch and synchronization defects in the CUDA kernel:

1. In stage_kda_proj, every CTA updates the same hidden residual and clears shared attn_out and moe_out buffers. The stage’s __syncthreads() calls synchronize only threads within each CTA; grid.sync() occurs after the stage, so CTAs can read and modify inconsistent residual and scratch values. 2. In stage_down, threads 144–255 return before the scratch-clear loops. Some projection-buffer indices therefore retain data from the previous layer, and the next KDA projection accumulates onto stale values.

The relevant residual update and clear ordering was:

for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < HIDDEN; i += blockDim.x) {
    float v = b2f(KP.hbuf[i]) + KP.attn_out[i] + KP.moe_out[i];
    KP.hbuf[i] = f2b(v);
}
__syncthreads();
rmsnorm_shared(KP.hbuf, KP.attn_norm[layer], smem, HIDDEN);
if (pid >= 72) return;
...
for (int i = threadIdx.x; i < HIDDEN; i += blockDim.x) {
    KP.attn_out[i] = 0.f;
    KP.moe_out[i] = 0.f;
}

For future implementations, make cross-CTA ownership and synchronization explicit at every shared-buffer phase boundary. Ensure all threads that own scratch-clear work reach the clear, and synchronize the grid before another stage consumes shared residuals or projection buffers. The official audit verdict is bug, correct=false, check_failed, with peak_fraction: null; no speedup should be inferred from this run.
